es.summary: Las hemorroides son venas inflamadas del ano o recto bajo, clasificadas en externas e internas. Aparecen por aumento de presión venosa y debilitamiento del tejido de soporte.
key_points: Presión venosa aumentada y tejido de soporte debilitado son la base fisiopatológica.
Factores de riesgo: estreñimiento, embarazo, esfuerzo, dieta baja en fibra y sedentarismo.
Síntomas externos: dolor, picor y bultos duros; internos: sangrado y prolapsos sin dolor.
El diagnóstico es clínico; se confirma con inspección y, de ser necesario, anoscopia.
Manejo inicial: dieta alta en fibra, hidratación, baños de asiento y tópicos antiinflamatorios.
Complicaciones incluyen trombosis, ulceración, sangrado profuso y estrangulación.

pathophysiology: Aumento de presión intraabdominal eleva la presión venosa perianal.
Las venas se dilatan y se inflaman, formando plexos hemorroidales.
El tejido conectivo que sostiene las venas se debilita con la edad o el embarazo.
En hemorroides internas, el plexo interno se prolapsa a través del canal anal.
risk_factors: Embarazo y aumento de progesterona que relaja la pared venosa.
Dieta baja en fibra y consumo insuficiente de agua.
Esfuerzo excesivo al defecar o levantar objetos pesados.
signs_symptoms: Hemorroide externa: picor, bulto duro, dolor al sentarse, posible sangrado superficial.
Hemorroide interna: sangrado rojo brillante al defecar, sensación de masa que puede prolapsar, sin dolor.
Sensación de presión o plenitud perianal.
Edema y eritema alrededor del ano.
diagnostics: Inspección visual del ano en posición de litotomía.
Palpación digital para identificar bultos externos o prolapsos internos.
Anoscopia o sigmoidoscopia si se sospecha patología interna compleja.
Resultados esperados: venas dilatadas, tejido inflamado, posible trombosis.
treatment: Aumento de fibra dietética (frutas, verduras, granos integrales) y 2‑3 L de agua/día.
Baños de asiento tibios 10‑15 min, 2‑3 veces al día.
Compresas frías para reducir edema y dolor.
Aplicación tópica de cremas con hidrocortisona, fenilefrina o witch‑hazel.
Laxantes suaves (p. ej., psyllium) si hay estreñimiento.
Procedimientos: ligadura con banda elástica, escleroterapia o cirugía en casos graves.
complications: Trombosis hemorroidal con dolor intenso y edema.
Ulceración y sangrado profuso que puede causar anemia.
Infección secundaria por irritación y ruptura de la piel.
Fístula perianal en casos de infección crónica.
nursing_care: Evaluar dolor (escala 0‑10), localización y factores desencadenantes.
Monitorear consistencia y frecuencia de deposiciones; registrar sangre en heces.
Inspeccionar piel perianal en cada turno; observar signos de infección.
Promover posición semisentada o uso de almohada para aliviar presión.
Aplicar compresas frías y recomendar baños de asiento según indicación.
Documentar respuesta a intervenciones y comunicar cambios al médico.
patient_teaching: Consumir ≥ 25 g de fibra diaria y beber al menos 2 L de agua.
Evitar esfuerzo excesivo; usar técnicas de defecación suaves (no retener respiración).
No permanecer más de 5 min en el inodoro; levantarse y caminar si necesita más tiempo.
Aplicar cremas tópicas según indicaciones y usar compresas frías cuando haya dolor.
Realizar baños de asiento tibios después de cada evacuación o según necesidad.
Buscar atención médica si hay sangrado abundante, dolor intenso o fiebre.

outcomes: Alivio del dolor: puntuación ≤ 3 en escala de 0‑10 en 48 h
Disminución del edema perianal observable en 72 h

interventions.action: Aplicar compresas frías en el área perianal 10‑20 min cada 2‑3 h
interventions.rationale: El frío produce vasoconstricción y reduce la inflamación y el dolor.

interventions.action: Realizar baños de asiento tibios 10‑15 min, 2‑3 veces al día
interventions.rationale: El calor aumenta el flujo sanguíneo y alivia la tensión muscular.

interventions.action: Administrar crema tópica con hidrocortisona según prescripción
interventions.rationale: Reduce la inflamación y el prurito local.

interventions.action: Enseñar al paciente técnicas de evacuación sin esfuerzo (posición semisentada, no retener respiración)
interventions.rationale: Disminuye la presión venosa y previene el aumento del dolor.

interventions.action: Evaluar dolor cada 4 h y registrar cambios
interventions.rationale: Permite ajustar intervenciones y asegurar control adecuado del dolor.

outcomes: Sin signos de infección (enrojecimiento, calor, supuración) en 7 días
Integridad de la piel perianal mantenida

interventions.action: Mantener higiene perianal suave con agua tibia y jabón neutro después de cada evacuación
interventions.rationale: Reduce la carga bacteriana y previene la irritación.

interventions.action: Secar delicadamente el área con toalla limpia o papel higiénico sin frotar
interventions.rationale: Evita microlesiones que facilitan la entrada de microorganismos.

interventions.action: Aplicar pomada antibacteriana o astringente (witch‑hazel) según indicación
interventions.rationale: Controla la flora cutánea y disminuye la inflamación.

interventions.action: Observar diariamente enrojecimiento, calor, edema o exudado y reportar al médico
interventions.rationale: Detección temprana permite intervención oportuna.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre evitar rascar o manipular la zona hemorroidal
interventions.rationale: Previene ruptura de la piel y colonización bacteriana.

en.summary: Hemorrhoids are inflamed veins of the anus or lower rectum, classified as external or internal. They appear due to increased venous pressure and weakening of supporting tissue.
key_points: Increased venous pressure and weakened support tissue are the pathophysiologic basis.
Risk factors: constipation, pregnancy, straining, low‑fiber diet, and sedentary lifestyle.
External symptoms: pain, itching, hard lumps; internal: bleeding and painless prolapse.
Diagnosis is clinical; confirmed with inspection and, if necessary, anoscopy.
Initial management: high‑fiber diet, hydration, sitz baths, and anti‑inflammatory topical agents.
Complications include thrombosis, ulceration, profuse bleeding, and strangulation.

pathophysiology: Increased intraabdominal pressure raises perianal venous pressure.
Veins dilate and inflame, forming hemorrhoidal plexuses.
Connective tissue supporting the veins weakens with age or pregnancy.
In internal hemorrhoids, the internal plexus prolapses through the anal canal.
risk_factors: Pregnancy and increased progesterone relaxing venous walls.
Low‑fiber diet and inadequate water intake.
Excessive straining during defecation or heavy lifting.
signs_symptoms: External hemorrhoid: itching, hard lump, pain when sitting, possible superficial bleeding.
Internal hemorrhoid: bright red bleeding during defecation, mass sensation that may prolapse, painless.
Feeling of pressure or fullness perianally.
Edema and erythema around the anus.
diagnostics: Visual inspection of the anus in lithotomy position.
Digital palpation to identify external lumps or internal prolapses.
Anoscopy or sigmoidoscopy if complex internal pathology suspected.
Expected findings: dilated veins, inflamed tissue, possible thrombosis.
treatment: Increase dietary fiber (fruits, vegetables, whole grains) and 2‑3 L of water/day.
Warm sitz baths 10‑15 min, 2‑3 times daily.
Cold compresses to reduce edema and pain.
Topical creams with hydrocortisone, phenylephrine, or witch‑hazel.
Gentle laxatives (e.g., psyllium) if constipation present.
Procedures: rubber band ligation, sclerotherapy, or surgery in severe cases.
complications: Hemorrhoidal thrombosis with intense pain and edema.
Ulceration and profuse bleeding that can cause anemia.
Secondary infection from irritation and skin rupture.
Perianal fistula in chronic infection cases.
nursing_care: Assess pain (0‑10 scale), location, and triggers.
Monitor stool consistency and frequency; record blood in stool.
Inspect perianal skin each shift; look for infection signs.
Promote semi‑sitting position or use a pillow to relieve pressure.
Apply cold compresses and recommend sitz baths as indicated.
Document response to interventions and communicate changes to the physician.
patient_teaching: Consume ≥ 25 g of fiber daily and drink at least 2 L of water.
Avoid excessive straining; use gentle defecation techniques (do not hold breath).
Do not stay on the toilet longer than 5 min; stand and walk if more time needed.
Apply topical creams as directed and use cold compresses when pain occurs.
Take warm sitz baths after each evacuation or as needed.
Seek medical care if there is heavy bleeding, intense pain, or fever.

outcomes: Pain relief: score ≤ 3 on 0‑10 scale within 48 h
Reduced perianal edema observable within 72 h

interventions.action: Apply cold compresses to the perianal area 10‑20 min every 2‑3 h
interventions.rationale: Cold causes vasoconstriction and reduces inflammation and pain.

interventions.action: Perform warm sitz baths 10‑15 min, 2‑3 times daily
interventions.rationale: Heat increases blood flow and relieves muscle tension.

interventions.action: Administer topical hydrocortisone cream as prescribed
interventions.rationale: Reduces inflammation and local itching.

interventions.action: Teach patient gentle evacuation techniques (semi‑sitting, no breath holding)
interventions.rationale: Decreases venous pressure and prevents pain escalation.

interventions.action: Assess pain every 4 h and record changes
interventions.rationale: Allows adjustment of interventions and ensures adequate pain control.

outcomes: No signs of infection (redness, warmth, drainage) within 7 days

interventions.action: Maintain gentle perianal hygiene with warm water and mild soap after each evacuation
interventions.rationale: Reduces bacterial load and prevents irritation.

interventions.action: Gently pat the area dry with a clean towel or non‑friction toilet paper
interventions.rationale: Avoids micro‑injuries that facilitate microbial entry.

interventions.action: Apply antibacterial or astringent ointment (witch‑hazel) as indicated
interventions.rationale: Controls skin flora and reduces inflammation.

interventions.action: Observe daily for redness, warmth, edema, or exudate and report to the physician
interventions.rationale: Early detection allows timely intervention.

interventions.action: Educate patient to avoid scratching or manipulating the hemorrhoidal area
interventions.rationale: Prevents skin rupture and bacterial colonization.

summary.0.quote: Hemorrhoids are swollen, inflamed veins around your anus or the lower part of your rectum .

key_points.2.quote: With internal hemorrhoids, you may have: Bleeding from your rectum - you would see bright red blood in your stool, on toilet paper, or in the toilet bowl after a bowel movement Prolapse, which is a hemorrhoid that has fallen through your anal opening Internal hemorrhoids are usually not painful unless they are prolapsed.

sections.pathophysiology.1.quote: Hemorrhoids are swollen, inflamed veins around your anus or the lower part of your rectum .

sections.pathophysiology.2.quote: Weakening of the supporting tissues in your anus and rectum. This can happen with aging and pregnancy .

sections.pathophysiology.3.quote: Prolapse, which is a hemorrhoid that has fallen through your anal opening

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: Progesterone relaxes the veins in the rectum, and the weight of the uterus causes more vasodilation.

sections.risk_factors.4.quote: Sitting on the toilet for long periods of time.

sections.signs_symptoms.1.quote: Internal hemorrhoids are usually not painful unless they are prolapsed.

sections.diagnostics.1.quote: Will do a digital rectal exam to check for internal hemorrhoids.

sections.diagnostics.2.quote: May do procedures such as an anoscopy to check for internal hemorrhoids.

sections.treatment.3.quote: Products with a combination of phenylephrine, glycerin, and petroleum ( Preparation H ), or a combination of hydrocortisone and bismuth ointment (Anusol) , are also recommended.

sections.treatment.4.quote: Pharmacologic measures to treat constipation start with adding psyllium (Metamucil) to a glass of juice or water and drinking it.

sections.nursing_care.2.quote: The nurse assesses the perineum, looking for any warning signs of infection, hematoma, or breakdown of laceration repair.

sections.nursing_care.4.quote: Sitz bath Speeds healing by increasing blood flow to the injured area, soothes pain, reduces inflammation, cleans perineum Prepare warm shallow bath; sit in water without soap and soak up to three times per day for 10–15 minutes.

sections.patient_teaching.5.quote: Instructions are given to call the health-care provider for: fever above 100.4° F (38º C) or chills pain upon urination shortness of breath unilateral extremity edema unusual facial edema headache not resolved with pain medication blurred vision heavy, bright red blood or clots saturating more than one pad in an hour foul-smelling lochia uterine tenderness or pain postpartum depression (crying, feelings of hopelessness, anger, disengaging with ne
